## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Rādhajātaka* (Ja 198) is a story in the canonical Pali *Jātaka* collection [SuttaCentral]. The narrative opens with the verse line *Pavāsā āgato tātā* ("I come, my son") [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. According to the commentary, the Buddha delivered the tale while dwelling at Jetavana regarding a backsliding monk (*ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu*) who had been stirred by passion after seeing an adorned woman [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In Burmese epigraphic and temple traditions, such as those cataloging Jātaka depictions, the name *Potthapāda Jātaka* is sometimes used instead, designating the story by the name of the younger parrot brother rather than the elder, Rādha [Ray 1946].
DharmaNexus identifies internal text reuse between the canonical verses of Ja 198 and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo), comprising six matching passages where the commentary embeds and explains the verses [DharmaNexus]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports any cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan traditions [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
